title: Carney’s South East Asian deals only a first step to expanding trade
html:
Prime Minister Mark Carney participates in the family photo with leaders at the opening ceremonies of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, Philippines, Nov. 15.Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

The effective completion of two trade deals last weekend in Manila reflects a growing commercial relationship between Canada and Southeast Asia, but a major expansion in trade will take time and sustained effort by Canadian businesses and governments in a diverse and often challenging region.

During his recent visit to the Philippines, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada had wrapped up bilateral trade negotiations with the country as well as the “substantial conclusion” of negotiations on a second trade deal with the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The fine print is still being worked out and the agreements are expected to be ratified next year.

Canada’s commercial ties with the region have grown notably in recent years. Exports of goods to the 11 ASEAN countries have doubled over the past decade hitting $11.6-billion in 2025, while imports have nearly tripled to $41-billion.

Still, that was only 1.5 per cent of total Canadian merchandise exports and 5.2 per cent of imports in 2025. And turning a region on the opposite side of the world into something more than a fringe market will require overcoming distance, a complex business environment, intense competition from other countries and a history of underengagement.

“We are playing catch-up, and we have a reputation in Southeast Asia among people in business and government and institutional elites … that our interest has been episodic, it’s waxed and waned,” said Jeff Nankivell, president and chief executive of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada.

He said Mr. Carney’s visits, increased business and governmental presence and the new trade deals are raising Canada’s profile. But that engagement needs to be sustained, he said: “If we ease off now, it would just reinforce the kind of bias that is there that Canadians are not serious about the region.”

Mr. Carney heralded the ASEAN deal as opening up a market of 700 million potential customers for Canadian exporters. The actual gains are more modest.

Canada already has a free-trade deal with four of the countries – Malaysia, Vietnam, Singapore, and Brunei – which are members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP). Last year, Ottawa negotiated a separate bilateral deal with Indonesia, the region’s largest and most important market.

Still, there’s value in signing a regional deal alongside bilateral agreements with the more important markets, Mr. Nankivell said. It will give Canadian companies baseline market access to several countries not already covered by trade deals, most notably Thailand and Cambodia, and facilitate the buildout of regional supply chains. It could also give Canadian firms a leg-up when competing for contracts in region-wide infrastructure projects, such as electrical grids, he said.

A 2017 feasibility report, prepared by Global Affairs Canada at the outset of Canada-ASEAN negotiations, estimated that a trade agreement could boost Canadian exports to the region by $2.67-billion annually, with the biggest gains coming from sales to countries not already covered by the CPTPP.

Mr. Carney said last week that the deal with the Philippines, which will grant preferential tariff treatment to 97 per cent of Canadian products, could triple exports to the country over the next decade. Canada exported $1-billion worth of goods to the Philippines in 2025, led by pork, wheat and wood products.

Wayne Farmer, president of the Canada-ASEAN Business Council (CABC), said the trade deals come at an opportune moment. The war in the Middle East has greatly disrupted energy supplies to the region and countries are looking for new sources of both conventional and clean energy – including possibly nuclear power.

Moreover, U.S. President Donald Trump’s heavy-handed approach to trade – Washington pressured Malaysia, Cambodia and Indonesia to sign agreements that curtail their ties with China – is making Canada more appealing.

“Canada is seen as a long-term trusted partner that doesn’t weaponize their trade for leverage,” Mr. Farmer said.

Several Southeast Asian companies are already big investors in Canadian energy export infrastructure. Malaysia’s state energy company Petronas owns a 25-per-cent stake in LNG Canada, and the Wood Fibre LNG terminal being built in Squamish is 70-per-cent owned by Indonesian billionaire Sukanto Tanoto’s RGE Group.

Carney sits beside Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and the Sultan of Brunei Hassanal Bolkiah, bottom left, during the opening ceremonies of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, Philippines, Nov. 15.Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press

Todd Winterhalt, senior vice-president of international markets at Export Development Canada, said he’s seen a notable uptick in Canadian business interest in the region. Some companies are selling into the market, while others are using it as a hub for low-cost manufacturing, sometimes in a bid to diversify their supply chains outside of China as part of what’s known as a “China Plus One” strategy.

Over the past three years, EDC has opened offices in Jakarta, Ho Chi Minh City, Manila and Bangkok, on top of the existing office in Singapore.

The export credit agency’s biggest book of business in the region is supporting Canadian agri-food companies, both commodity exporters and businesses providing food processing and storage equipment, Mr. Winterhalt said. But EDC is increasingly helping clean-tech, digital and defence companies find opportunities as well. “It’s fair to say that it started from a low base, but it is seeing very strong growth,” he said.

While there is momentum, that doesn’t mean Southeast Asia is about to become a major market for Canada.

In a few areas, Canadian companies have a significant toehold. National Bank of Canada owns Cambodia’s largest bank, ABA Bank, and insurance companies Sunlife and Manulife have been major players in the region for over a century. But in many industries, Canadian businesses looking to enter the market will be competing against Chinese, American, Japanese, European and Australian firms with much deeper ties.

Southeast Asia can also be a difficult place to do business. A CABC survey published this year noted that Canadian businesses “continue to encounter regulatory uncertainty, complex or costly customs procedures, corruption and nepotism, non-tariff measures, differing standards and high transport costs.”

That said, the survey also found significant optimism, with 83 per cent of respondents saying they planned to increase their trade and investment in the region over the next five years.

Julie Nguyen, chair of Canada-ASEAN Initiatives at York University and director of the Canada-Vietnam Trade Council, said that signing a trade deal is just the beginning. Expanding commercial ties will require extended, on-the-ground engagement.

“Asian partners will not do business right away. It might take two years, five years to build that trust before they actually do business with you,” she said.

Canada does have a built-in advantage, she added. There are around 1.5 million Canadians of Southeast Asian heritage, including around one million people of Filipino heritage and around 300,000 people of Vietnamese heritage.

“They can play a big role in building those relationships before we can actually do business or get a contract with an Asian partner,” Prof. Nguyen said.
summary: Turning a region on the opposite side of the world into something more than a fringe market will require time and sustained effort
